case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA preempts a state-law failure-to-warn claim when EPA has affirmatively determined the warning is not required and the manufacturer cannot add it to the pesticide label without EPA approval.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. § 136 et seq., especially the express preemption clause in 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b) (states may not impose labeling or packaging requirements in addition to or different from FIFRA).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues that the plaintiff’s state-law failure-to-warn claim functions as a state-imposed "labeling requirement" that is "in addition to or different from" EPA’s FIFRA-approved labeling determinations. Because EPA has determined the specific warning is not required and FIFRA makes it unlawful to sell a pesticide with labeling that departs from the EPA-approved label, Monsanto contends it was legally impossible to comply with both state tort duties (to add the warning) and federal law (which forbids unapproved label changes). Monsanto also emphasizes that allowing juries to require warnings EPA rejected would defeat FIFRA’s objective of nationally uniform pesticide labeling and create inconsistent obligations across states.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues that FIFRA does not preempt traditional state tort duties unless the state duty truly imposes a labeling obligation that is "in addition to or different from" federal requirements, and that a damages verdict is not itself a state "requirement" to alter labels in the way FIFRA preempts. He further contends that manufacturers can seek EPA approval to strengthen warnings and thus can comply with both federal law and state-law duties; in his view, EPA registration and labeling decisions set a regulatory floor and do not categorically bar additional warnings where warranted. He also argues that Congress preserved a role for state remedies and that preemption should not be inferred from EPA’s views unless EPA action carries the force of law clearly disallowing the warning at issue.
key_precedents: Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor raise the strongest objection: we should not treat EPA’s view that a warning is “not required” as a free-floating federal prohibition, or else §136v(b) risks becoming broad tort immunity untethered to concrete federal law. But here, as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, the state-law verdict turns on the absence of a specific warning not contained in the EPA-approved, product-specific label, and FIFRA forbids unilateral label deviation absent prior EPA approval—so the damages duty functions as an additional/different labeling “requirement” at the point of sale under Bates. The availability of a later petition process does not eliminate that present collision; it only underscores that the lawful route for change runs through EPA, not a jury. The narrow and institutionally sound course is to ground preemption in demonstrated, case-specific EPA label approval with legal effect and to leave room for parallel misbranding-type claims where EPA has not actually resolved the warning question in that binding way.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that an EPA “not required” view, standing alone, may lack force of law and so cannot itself supply preemptive effect. But that framing does not meet the operative contradiction: FIFRA makes it unlawful to sell a pesticide with labeling that differs from the EPA-approved label absent prior EPA approval, and (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize) a state failure-to-warn verdict premised on the absence of a specific warning operates as a state labeling “requirement” under Bates. At the time of sale, the manufacturer cannot simultaneously comply with a state duty to add the warning now and a federal prohibition on unilateral label changes now—later petitioning EPA does not erase that present logical contradiction. Because §136v(b)’s text bars state “requirements … in addition to or different from” federal labeling requirements, pre-emption follows here without relying on freestanding agency policy or “purposes and objectives” speculation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that EPA’s statement that a warning is “not required” is not, standing alone, a freestanding federal prohibition, and that a petition-and-amendment route might have tested the matter. But §136v(b) asks whether the state rule imposes a labeling “requirement … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and under Bates the state-law damages duty here operates as such a “requirement” because liability turns on the absence of warning language not included in the EPA-approved label. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, FIFRA independently makes it unlawful to sell with labeling that departs from the approved label absent prior EPA authorization; the mere availability of a petition process does not eliminate the present, concrete collision at the point of sale when a jury-imposed duty would compel different labeling before EPA has approved it. Allowing state verdicts to function as de facto label mandates in these circumstances risks the Buckman-type interference with a sensitive and highly technical federal labeling regime that Congress protected through express preemption.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Petitioners’ strongest point—pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan—is that, under Bates, a tort verdict may operate as a state “requirement,” and FIFRA generally bars unilateral deviation from an EPA-approved label at the point of sale. But §136v(b) pre-empts only state requirements “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and an EPA-approved label that omits a warning (or an agency view that a warning is “not required”) is not, without more, a federal requirement prohibiting that warning. As Justice Barrett underscores, Petitioners have not shown a concrete, binding EPA action with force of law rejecting the precise warning at issue (or a denial after Monsanto sought approval), so the asserted “logical contradiction” described by Justice Thomas remains speculative rather than demonstrated impossibility. Treating federal nonrequirement as categorical preemption would improperly expand FIFRA’s targeted express preemption into broad tort immunity and would unduly foreclose potentially meritorious parallel misbranding-type claims that Bates preserves.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor raise the hardest objection: a federal “not required” determination should not automatically become a federal “forbidden,” lest §136v(b) metastasize into broad tort immunity. But the preemption analysis here can rest on enacted text and the concrete structure of FIFRA label approval, as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas stress: at the point of sale, federal law makes it unlawful to market with labeling that materially departs from the EPA-approved label absent prior EPA authorization, and the state failure-to-warn verdict operates (under Bates) as a labeling “requirement” demanding different language now. The availability of a petition process does not erase that present incompatibility; it instead confirms that the only lawful route to add the warning is via EPA, not via a state jury’s mandate. Cabining the holding to product-specific EPA-approved labeling and leaving room for Bates “parallel” misbranding-type claims where EPA has not actually resolved the warning issue avoids the tort-immunity slippery slope Barrett identifies while applying §136v(b) as written.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s (and Justice Sotomayor’s) strongest point is that an agency’s view that a warning is “not required” cannot, standing alone, be treated as a free-floating federal prohibition, lest we convert a narrow express preemption clause into broad tort immunity. But the text Congress enacted in §136v(b) asks whether the state rule imposes labeling “requirements … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and under Bates a damages verdict can operate as such a requirement when liability turns on the absence of specific label language. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, FIFRA makes it unlawful to sell with labeling that departs from the EPA-approved label absent prior EPA approval; a state-law duty that effectively demands an immediate different warning therefore collides with federal law at the point of sale, and the speculative prospect of later petitioning EPA does not eliminate that present contradiction. Anchoring the holding, as Chief Justice Roberts suggests, to the concrete fact of EPA’s product-specific label approval (rather than to general agency “views”) respects both the statute’s express preemption text and Bates’s recognition of “parallel” claims where state law merely tracks federal misbranding duties.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor press the best counterpoint: an EPA statement that a warning is “not required” does not automatically equal a force-of-law federal prohibition, and pre-emption should not become sweeping tort immunity on an underdeveloped record. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, the operative statutory conflict here is not an abstract “EPA view”; it is FIFRA’s concrete rule that the product may not be sold with labeling that materially deviates from the EPA-approved label absent prior EPA approval, coupled with Bates’s recognition that a failure-to-warn verdict functions as a state “requirement.” The state-law duty’s primary driver is to compel a cancer warning not on the approved label at the time of sale, which is “different from” the federal labeling requirement within the meaning of §136v(b), and the availability of a later petition process does not eliminate that present collision or the significant interference with the federally conferred uniform-label regime. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that we should cabin the holding to cases with a demonstrated, product-specific EPA label approval addressing the warning issue and preserve Bates-style parallel claims where EPA has not affirmatively resolved the warning question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I remain unpersuaded that Petitioners have carried their burden to show the state verdict imposed a labeling “requirement … different from” any federal “requirement” within the meaning of §136v(b), rather than simply one not federally required. The Chief Justice, Justice Kagan, and Justice Thomas emphasize the point-of-sale illegality of unilateral label deviations and characterize that as a present “logical contradiction,” but that framing still depends on a demonstrated federal prohibition of the particular cancer warning the jury supposedly required—not merely the absence of it on an approved label. On this record, there is no force-of-law EPA action rejecting that specific warning (nor a shown denial after Monsanto pursued the amendment route), so the asserted conflict remains speculative in the way Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson describe, and reading “not required” as “forbidden” risks expanding FIFRA’s express preemption into broad tort immunity. Under State Farm-style review principles we routinely apply, I am reluctant to infer a dispositive federal resolution where the agency has not clearly and concretely made one as to the precise warning at issue.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I accept the Petitioners’ strongest point, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, that a failure-to-warn damages verdict can operate as a state “requirement,” and that FIFRA generally prohibits selling with labeling that materially departs from the EPA-approved label absent prior EPA authorization. But that does not itself resolve §136v(b)’s enacted question—whether the state duty is “in addition to or different from” a federal “requirement”—because, as Justice Barrett emphasizes, this record does not show a binding, product-specific EPA determination with force of law that rejected (and thereby legally foreclosed) the particular warning the jury found necessary. Treating EPA’s nonrequirement (or silence) as an affirmative federal prohibition would transform FIFRA’s targeted preemption clause into broad tort immunity and would sidestep the statute’s EPA-centered mechanisms for label revision that Congress designed to mediate federal–state authority. Without proof of a concrete federal “no,” the claimed conflict remains speculative, and I would not extend preemption beyond what the text and structure, as understood in Bates, support.

John Roberts.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars States from imposing labeling requirements “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and under Bates common-law duties can qualify as such requirements when they effectively demand a different label. Here EPA has affirmatively determined the specific warning is not required, and FIFRA’s implementing scheme makes it unlawful to sell a pesticide with labeling that departs from the EPA-approved label absent prior EPA approval—so a state-law verdict premised on the absence of that warning would operate as a nonparallel, additional labeling requirement. A narrow holding respects federalism while preserving institutional legitimacy: where EPA has made a formal, case-specific no-warning determination and the manufacturer cannot unilaterally add the warning, the state failure-to-warn claim is preempted, without foreclosing traditional tort claims that merely enforce FIFRA-parallel misbranding duties.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, the only proper question is whether the federal and state rules are in direct conflict—i.e., in logical contradiction. Here, the state failure-to-warn claim operates as a state “requirement for labeling” (as Bates recognized) demanding a cancer warning that EPA has affirmatively determined is not required on the FIFRA-approved label, while FIFRA makes it unlawful to sell a pesticide with labeling that departs from the approved labeling without EPA approval; those commands cannot both be satisfied at the same time. The possibility that the manufacturer could petition EPA for a label change does not eliminate the contradiction when federal law, as applied, forbids unilateral compliance with the state-imposed duty. Because §136v(b) expressly prohibits state labeling requirements “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s, and this state duty would add precisely such a requirement, the claim is pre-empted without resort to any freewheeling “purposes and objectives” inquiry.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FIFRA contains an express preemption clause barring States from imposing any “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” those required under federal law, and a state-law failure-to-warn verdict here would operate as just such a labeling requirement by demanding a cancer warning that EPA has affirmatively found not required. Unlike a truly “parallel” claim that enforces a federal misbranding or labeling duty, this claim rests on the premise that Monsanto should have altered its label notwithstanding EPA’s contrary determination, so it is not “fully consistent with” FIFRA’s labeling regime under Bates. Allowing a jury to impose liability for adhering to an EPA-approved label also creates a concrete risk of disrupting a sensitive, highly technical federal registration-and-labeling process by substituting state tort judgments for EPA’s expert determination, and preemption analysis should be driven by the statute’s text rather than generalized appeals to state remedial interests. Because Monsanto cannot unilaterally add the demanded warning without EPA approval, the state duty as applied would compel labeling “in addition to or different from” what FIFRA requires and is therefore preempted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, so I begin with that text and our instruction in Bates that common-law duties are preempted only to the extent they impose a genuinely divergent labeling requirement. On these facts, EPA’s registration and its view that a particular warning is “not required” do not, without more, establish that federal law affirmatively forbids the warning such that the state duty necessarily compels a label “different from” FIFRA’s; the manufacturer can seek EPA approval to strengthen warnings, and a damages verdict does not itself operate as a state labeling code. Treating EPA’s nonrequirement determination as categorically preemptive would risk converting FIFRA’s narrow express preemption into broad immunity and screening out potentially meritorious claims absent a clear federal prohibition carrying the force of law. If Monsanto can show, under Albrecht’s framework, that EPA actually made a legally binding decision rejecting this precise warning such that approval was not possible, that would alter the analysis, but on the present premise of mere nonrequirement the claim is not preempted.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with enacted text: FIFRA expressly bars States from imposing any “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates makes clear that common-law duties enforced through damages actions count as such “requirements.” Here EPA has affirmatively approved Roundup’s label and determined the specific cancer warning is not required; on these facts, a state failure-to-warn verdict would necessarily demand a label change that diverges from the pesticide-specific federal labeling determination, not merely a parallel obligation. Nor can the State avoid preemption by pointing to the possibility of seeking EPA approval, because the relevant federal scheme makes it unlawful to sell with unapproved labeling and—given EPA’s contrary determination—imposes a concrete federal obstacle to the state-imposed duty as applied. I would not infer a broad state remedial carveout from congressional silence or agency “views”; what matters is that the statutory “Uniformity” provision, as implemented through EPA’s actual label decision here, squarely conflicts with the state-law labeling requirement the plaintiff seeks to enforce.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Start with the text: FIFRA expressly forbids States from imposing any “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, §136v(b). On these facts, EPA has affirmatively approved a Roundup label without the cancer warning and has indicated the warning is not required; a state-law failure-to-warn verdict would operate as a state-imposed “requirement” to add that very warning, making the state duty “different from” the federal labeling determination. And because FIFRA makes it unlawful to sell a pesticide with labeling that departs from the EPA-approved label absent EPA approval, the state verdict would press the manufacturer to do what federal law bars unless and until EPA authorizes it—an outcome we should not manufacture from ambiguity when Congress supplied an express preemption rule aimed at national labeling uniformity. Under a clear-statement approach, a “parallel requirements” theory cannot survive where the agency with exclusive labeling authority has actually determined the warning is unwarranted; the state claim seeks to impose an additional/different label obligation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Start with FIFRA’s text: § 136v(b) sets the default rule that States may not impose “any requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates recognizes that common-law failure-to-warn duties can be such “requirements” unless they are genuinely parallel to FIFRA. On these facts, EPA has affirmatively determined the specific warning is not required and the manufacturer may not add it to the label without EPA approval; a state-law verdict effectively compelling that warning would therefore be a non-parallel, additional labeling requirement. Even if the manufacturer could theoretically ask EPA for permission, the state rule still significantly interferes with the federally conferred discretion and uniformity FIFRA protects by letting juries override EPA’s considered labeling judgment and create state-by-state label mandates. Because the state duty’s core driver is to force a label change beyond (and contrary to) the EPA-approved label, FIFRA preempts the claim.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: On this record, Monsanto’s preemption theory depends on a factual/legal premise it did not establish: that EPA would have rejected (and legally barred) the specific cancer warning Durnell’s state-law theory would require, rather than approving it upon request. Under the usual preservation and burden principles, the challenger must show a material conflict—i.e., that compliance with both federal law and the state duty was impossible—and Monsanto’s failure to seek EPA approval leaves that conflict speculative rather than demonstrated. Applying the State Farm-style “path may reasonably be discerned” approach to the agency side of the story, the materials described show EPA’s general view on glyphosate but do not, in this case posture, amount to a concrete, force-of-law determination forbidding the precise warning at issue. Consistent with Bates, a failure-to-warn claim is not expressly preempted unless it imposes a labeling requirement “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s; absent a shown federal prohibition on adding the warning through FIFRA’s process, Durnell’s claim is best treated as parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding/warning standards rather than different from them.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with FIFRA’s text and structure, §136v(b) expressly preempts only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, while FIFRA otherwise preserves a substantial role for state regulation and remedies—so the key question is whether this particular failure-to-warn claim would impose a nonparallel, label-based duty. Under Bates, a state-law tort duty is preempted only insofar as it would require a label change that conflicts with FIFRA’s misbranding/labeling requirements; on this record, EPA’s view that the warning is “not required” does not, by itself, establish that FIFRA forbids Monsanto from proposing a strengthened warning through the statute’s EPA-centered amendment process. Because the manufacturer can seek EPA approval for additional warnings, the asserted “impossibility” conflict is not shown with the kind of clear, force-of-law federal prohibition that would make the state duty categorically “different from” FIFRA rather than potentially parallel to it. Given FIFRA’s calibrated scheme—national labeling oversight by EPA without an across-the-board displacement of traditional state remedies—I would hold the claim not expressly preempted on these facts.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars a state-law failure-to-warn claim when EPA has registered the pesticide label without the requested warning and federal law requires EPA approval before adding that warning to the label.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. § 136 et seq., especially the express preemption provision in 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b) (states may not impose labeling/packaging requirements “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s requirements).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues that the Missouri failure-to-warn verdict necessarily imposes a state “labeling requirement” that is “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, because EPA has determined the challenged label is acceptable without the additional warning and, as a practical and legal matter, Monsanto cannot unilaterally add the warning without prior EPA approval. Under Monsanto’s view, a tort judgment compelling a warning functions as a state labeling mandate and is therefore expressly preempted by § 136v(b); allowing such claims would defeat FIFRA’s goal of nationally uniform labeling, force regulated parties into conflicting obligations, and let juries second-guess EPA’s scientific/regulatory determinations.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues that FIFRA does not preempt traditional state tort claims unless they would require a label that directly conflicts with FIFRA’s own requirements; a state-law duty to provide adequate warnings can parallel (rather than add to or differ from) federal misbranding and labeling standards. He contends that EPA registration is not a definitive federal determination that no additional warning is warranted for all purposes and that manufacturers can seek EPA approval (and in some circumstances use mechanisms to add or strengthen warnings) so compliance with both state tort duties and FIFRA is not impossible. On this view, § 136v(b) preempts state positive-law labeling rules but not damages actions that simply enforce a congruent duty not to sell misbranded products with inadequate warnings.
key_precedents: Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, 544 U.S. 431 (2005)
Cipollone v. Liggett Group, Inc., 505 U.S. 504 (1992)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Bates preserves genuinely parallel state duties and that an EPA-approved label is not necessarily an affirmative federal prohibition on stronger warnings. But §136v(b) must be read in the context of FIFRA’s integrated, EPA-centered labeling scheme: a Missouri verdict premised on the absence of a specific cancer warning operates as a state-imposed “requirement for labeling … in addition to or different from” the federally approved label the manufacturer must use unless and until EPA approves a change. As Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett explain, the availability of a petition process does not eliminate the present conflict; it confirms Congress’s choice to channel labeling judgments through EPA rather than through fifty juries. Extending Bates’s “parallel” path to encompass this application would risk nullifying §136v(b)’s specific command by allowing States to impose, through damages, what they cannot impose directly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that §136v(b) preempts only non-parallel duties and that EPA’s prior approval does not, by itself, amount to an affirmative federal prohibition on additional warnings. But the question under the Supremacy Clause is whether the state judgment “impose[d]” a labeling “requirement[] … in addition to or different from” federal law, and—per the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh—a verdict predicated on the absence of a cancer warning operates as a present mandate to alter the label notwithstanding FIFRA’s command that the registrant use the EPA-approved label unless and until EPA approves a change. That creates a logical contradiction in operation: state law demands liability unless the label is changed now, while federal law withholds authority to make that change unilaterally now. The availability of a future petition to EPA does not negate the present additional requirement the state judgment imposes, nor does it convert the verdict into a genuinely “parallel” duty under Bates.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s central point—that EPA registration is a floor and that Monsanto could seek EPA approval for stronger warnings—does not answer the operative question under the Supremacy Clause and FIFRA’s express text. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, the Missouri verdict functions as a state-imposed “requirement for labeling” that is “in addition to or different from” the federally approved label, because it predicates liability on the absence of specific warning language that Monsanto may not lawfully add unilaterally absent EPA approval. Bates preserves only genuinely parallel duties; a jury mandate to add a particular cancer warning not required by federal law, and not presently permissible without prior federal action, is not parallel in application but additional. Anchoring the analysis in §136v(b)’s enacted terms avoids the sort of freewheeling “objectives” inquiry that would treat general federal purposes, rather than concrete statutory commands, as preemptive law.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point that a damages verdict can functionally pressure a label change, but §136v(b) asks whether the State has imposed a labeling “requirement[] … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, not whether the verdict might induce the manufacturer to pursue a different label. Under Bates, a common-law duty that tracks FIFRA’s own misbranding prohibition is not “different from” federal law merely because EPA previously approved a label without the warning; converting EPA’s approval into a categorical ceiling would erase Bates’s parallel-duty path without a clear congressional command. Justice Barrett’s administrability concern cannot supply the missing textual link from “different from” to “not yet EPA-approved,” especially where FIFRA’s structure contemplates that registrants may seek amended warnings through EPA rather than being locked into a single, federally mandated label forever. On this record, Petitioners have not shown the requisite concrete contradiction—an affirmative federal determination forbidding the warning—necessary to displace this traditional damages action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh make the best point for Petitioner: a tort verdict can operate as a practical inducement to change a label, and FIFRA channels label changes through EPA. But §136v(b) does not preempt every state rule that pressures a different label; it preempts only state “requirements” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates tells us a state duty genuinely tracking FIFRA’s misbranding standard is not “different from” federal law. The missing step in Petitioners’ position is an affirmative federal prohibition on the cancer warning (or a showing that EPA approval is legally unavailable), because otherwise the argument collapses “different from” into “not already on the registered label,” turning EPA’s prior approval into a ceiling Congress did not enact. Justice Gorsuch’s administrability rule—preemption whenever the manufacturer cannot act unilaterally—adds an extra-textual hurdle and effectively reads Bates’s parallel-duty pathway out of the statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Bates preserves genuinely parallel state duties and that “not yet approved” is not the same as “forbidden,” so we should not treat EPA registration as a categorical ceiling. But §136v(b) asks whether the State has “impose[d]” a “requirement[] for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain) a damages verdict predicated on the absence of a cancer warning functions as a present labeling command that differs from the EPA-approved label the manufacturer must use unless and until EPA approves a change. The availability of a petition process does not cure what the judgment imposes now; it instead confirms Congress’s choice to channel label-content decisions through EPA rather than through state juries. Extending Bates’s “parallel” category to cover a state-law duty that necessarily demands label language beyond what federal law presently permits the manufacturer to adopt would drain §136v(b)’s specific prohibition of operative effect.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Bates preserves genuinely parallel state duties and that mere absence of a warning on an EPA-approved label should not itself equal a federal prohibition. But the decisive feature here is operational: as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the Missouri verdict predicates liability on the absence of a specific cancer warning that Monsanto cannot add to the label unilaterally without prior EPA approval, so the judgment functions as a state-imposed “requirement[] for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements under §136v(b). The availability of a later petition to EPA does not eliminate what the state judgment “imposes” now; it instead confirms Congress’s choice to channel label-content decisions through EPA rather than through state juries. Accepting respondent’s framing would collapse §136v(b) into a general misbranding standard enforceable via 50 different jury specifications, which is inconsistent with the administrable line Congress drew and Bates’s parallel-duty limitation in application.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the case’s hardest point: under Bates, a state duty that truly tracks FIFRA’s misbranding standard is not preempted merely because EPA previously approved a label without the warning. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, this Missouri verdict is not operating at the level of a general “do not misbrand” parallel duty; it is being applied as a concrete requirement to add a particular cancer warning to the label—something Monsanto cannot lawfully implement unilaterally while the EPA-approved label remains in force. On this record, that makes the state-law duty, as applied, a “requirement for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements within §136v(b), and the ability to petition EPA does not cure the present displacement of EPA’s exclusive role in setting the label. I therefore do not see a principled way to characterize this as “parallel” without effectively turning Bates into a vehicle for nullifying §136v(b)’s text in cases where liability is pegged to the absence of specific label language.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point—that a tort verdict can function as a de facto labeling mandate within FIFRA’s EPA-centered scheme—is the strongest case for preemption here. But §136v(b) preempts only state “requirements” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates directs courts to ask whether the state duty is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard, not to treat any verdict that would induce a label change as categorically “different from” the approved label. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s framing still assumes the dispositive premise—that the EPA-approved label operates as an affirmative federal command forbidding the additional warning—when, on this record, FIFRA’s structure (including routes to seek strengthened warnings) cuts against finding the concrete contradiction necessary for conflict preemption (i.e., state law prohibiting what federal law requires). Absent a showing that federal law actually forbade the warning or made it legally impossible to secure EPA approval, I do not see a textual basis to displace this traditional damages action at the threshold.

John Roberts.reasoning: Reading § 136v(b) in context and within FIFRA’s integrated scheme of EPA-centered label approval, a state-law failure-to-warn verdict that effectively compels Monsanto to add a cancer warning operates as a state “labeling requirement” imposed “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, because FIFRA makes label content subject to EPA control and does not allow unilateral additions of the demanded warning absent EPA approval. The respondent’s “parallel duty” theory cannot be applied so broadly that it nullifies § 136v(b)’s specific command and the Act’s national-uniformity design: a jury-imposed duty to add a warning that EPA has registered the product without (and, on this record, has treated as scientifically unwarranted or misleading) is not “genuinely equivalent” to FIFRA’s requirements for that product. Allowing such claims would convert general state tort principles into de facto state labeling regimes, precisely what § 136v(b) forbids, and would invite conflicting obligations where federal law interposes EPA as the necessary decisionmaker on label warnings. On these facts, the claim is expressly preempted because it demands a label change that federal law assigns to EPA and that the federal registration/approval framework has not required.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause’s original meaning, preemption turns on whether the State has imposed a “requirement” that is in logical contradiction with federal law. Here, Missouri’s failure-to-warn verdict functions as a state-law labeling requirement compelling Monsanto to add a cancer warning, yet FIFRA makes it unlawful to distribute a pesticide with labeling not approved by EPA and EPA has registered the product without that warning—so Monsanto cannot simultaneously satisfy the state-imposed duty and the federal prohibition without first obtaining EPA approval. Because the relevant preemptive rule is statutory (FIFRA § 136v(b)’s bar on state “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements), and not mere agency “policy,” the direct-conflict inquiry is satisfied on these facts. Missouri’s duty is not genuinely “parallel” to a federal requirement when the added warning is not required by federal law for this product and cannot be unilaterally adopted consistent with the federal labeling regime.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause supplies a rule of decision only where a valid federal enactment actually imposes a right or restriction that conflicts with what state law demands; here that work is done by FIFRA’s express preemption clause, § 136v(b), which forbids any state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements. On these facts, the Missouri failure-to-warn verdict necessarily operates as a state-imposed labeling requirement because it would obligate Monsanto to add a specific warning that is not on the EPA-registered label, while federal law requires EPA approval before that warning may be added—creating an impermissible additional state labeling obligation rather than a merely parallel duty. This conclusion rests on statutory text, not a freewheeling inquiry into federal purposes: once § 136v(b) is applied according to its terms, a damages judgment compelling a different label is barred. To the extent EPA’s registration reflects an agency-approved label content that excludes the requested warning and the manufacturer cannot unilaterally add it, the state-law duty conflicts with the federal restriction and must give way.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 136v(b) preempts only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s own requirements, and under Bates common-law duties are preempted only when they impose non-parallel labeling obligations. EPA’s registration decision, standing alone, does not clearly command that no additional cancer warning may ever be required; it reflects that the label satisfied federal minimum standards at the time, not that federal law affirmatively forbids strengthening the warning in response to evolving risk evidence. Reading §136v(b) to treat every tort verdict seeking an additional warning as automatically “different from” federal law would overextend the text and create an overbroad preclusive effect disconnected from whether the state duty truly conflicts with FIFRA’s misbranding prohibition (i.e., a parallel duty not to market a product with inadequate warnings). And because Monsanto can seek EPA approval (and, in some circumstances, pursue label changes through federally provided mechanisms), the case is not one where federal law specifically prescribes a course leaving “no rightful option” but to keep the existing label, so the state failure-to-warn claim is not categorically barred by the express preemption clause on these facts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with the enacted text: §136v(b) preempts only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s own requirements, and under Bates a common-law failure-to-warn claim survives when it enforces a duty genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard (i.e., not to sell a product with labeling that is false or misleading or that omits necessary warnings). EPA registration, standing alone, does not rewrite §136v(b)’s test by converting every registered label into a federal command that no further warning may be required for all purposes; absent an affirmative statutory or regulatory determination that FIFRA forbids the warning Durnell says state law required, Monsanto’s argument relies too much on implied “uniformity” and agency action rather than the statute’s actual preemption line. Read in FIFRA’s structure, Congress preserved a role for States while barring only divergent state labeling rules, so a damages verdict based on a parallel inadequacy-of-warning theory is not automatically “in addition to or different from” federal law. And to the extent Monsanto’s argument sounds in impossibility, it turns on whether federal law actually prohibited seeking and obtaining approval for a strengthened warning—not on a heightened clear-statement demand or on treating registration as categorical preclusion of state tort duties.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FIFRA’s enacted text squarely provides that a State “shall not impose” any “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” those required under the Act. A state-law failure-to-warn verdict here operates as a labeling “requirement” because it turns on the content of the EPA-approved label and, as applied, demands an added warning the agency has not required and that federal law does not allow Monsanto to add unilaterally without prior EPA approval. Under the common-law baseline, tort duties can function as regulatory requirements when they effectively command particular label language; absent a clear statutory instruction preserving that power in the face of §136v(b)’s uniformity command, we must respect Congress’s express preemption rule. Bates permits only genuinely “parallel” duties, and on these facts—where the requested warning would change the EPA-registered label rather than match an existing FIFRA requirement—the Missouri judgment imposes an additional/different labeling requirement and is preempted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The statutory trigger is FIFRA’s express preemption clause: a State may not “impose” any “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s requirements, and Bates holds that common-law duties and verdicts can qualify as such “requirements.” On these facts, EPA has registered the product with the challenged label and federal law generally forbids Monsanto from unilaterally adding the requested warning without prior EPA approval; a Missouri failure-to-warn verdict therefore operates in practice as a state-imposed labeling mandate that displaces the federally approved label and significantly constrains the federally conferred discretion to use the EPA-approved label nationwide. That state-law regime is not merely “parallel” enforcement of FIFRA’s misbranding standard; it compels a different label than the one federal law currently allows the manufacturer to use, thereby creating the kind of additional/different labeling requirement §136v(b) forbids. The better administrable rule, consistent with the text and with Bates, is that when compliance with a state tort duty necessarily requires altering an EPA-approved label in a way the manufacturer cannot implement without federal approval, the state duty is preempted as an additional/different “requirement for labeling.”

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bates, a state-law failure-to-warn verdict is a “requirement for labeling,” and it survives § 136v(b) only if it is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding/labeling requirements rather than “in addition to or different from” them. Here, EPA registered the Roundup label without the cancer warning plaintiff says Missouri law required, and (on this record) Monsanto could not lawfully add that warning unilaterally without prior EPA approval—so the jury’s judgment functionally imposed a different labeling requirement than the federally approved one. Given that FIFRA channels label content through EPA’s approval process to achieve national uniformity, it is not arbitrary to treat a tort duty compelling an EPA-unapproved warning as barred where it would force the manufacturer into a labeling change that federal law does not permit absent EPA action. On these case-specific facts, the state duty is not “parallel” in the Bates sense because it operates to override EPA’s label determination rather than merely enforce it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with FIFRA’s text, §136v(b) expressly preempts only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s own requirements; under Bates, state tort duties are preempted only to the extent they impose a non-parallel labeling standard. On these facts, EPA’s registration of Monsanto’s label—without more—does not itself establish that federal law affirmatively requires the absence of the requested cancer warning, so Monsanto has not shown a concrete Supremacy Clause conflict in the sense that state law “prohibits what federal law requires.” Because FIFRA’s structure contemplates ongoing label regulation and the possibility of seeking EPA approval for strengthened warnings, a state failure-to-warn verdict that tracks FIFRA’s misbranding/adequate-warning baseline can operate as a parallel requirement rather than an “additional or different” one. Absent a clear federal determination that the warning is forbidden (not merely unapproved at the time of registration), the express-preemption clause does not categorically bar this traditional damages action.
